ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: Sujay and Rishabh are taking turns marking lattice points within a square board in the Cartesian plane with opposite vertices $(1, 1)$,$(n, n)$ for some constant $n$. Sujay loses when the two-point pattern $P$ below shows up. That is, Sujay loses when there exists a pair of points $(x, y)$ and $(x + 2, y + 1)$. He and Rishabh stop marking points when the pattern $P$ appears on the board. If Rishabh goes first, let $S$ be the set of all integers $3 \le n \le 100$ such that Rishabh has a strategy to always trick Sujay into being the one who creates $P$. Find the sum of all elements of $S$.\n<image1>

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the grid diagram in the attached figure there are two black grid points; one point is horizontally separated from the other point by 2 units and vertically separated by 1 unit, therefore the forbidden two-point pattern P shown in the figure is the two-point pattern composed of the grid points (x,y) and (x+2,y+1). Reasoning: Let the chessboard grid point set be B_n={1,...,n}×{1,...,n}. Use the 180-degree rotation pairing rho(x,y)=(n+1-x,n+1-y). If the difference vector of the two points is (2,1), after rotation the difference vector of the two points is (-2,-1), which as an unordered two-point pattern is still the same forbidden pattern, so rho preserves the forbidden relation. Also any point v=(x,y) and its rotated point rho(v) will not themselves form the forbidden pattern, because rho(v)-v=(n+1-2x,n+1-2y); when n is even the two coordinate differences are odd, so the first coordinate cannot be ±2; when n is odd the two coordinate differences are even, so the second coordinate cannot be ±1. Therefore paired points will not directly form P. If n is even, rho has no fixed point. Sujay can adopt a response strategy: whenever Rishabh safely marks v, Sujay marks rho(v). Before Sujay responds, the already marked set remains rotationally symmetric; if rho(v) would form P with some old point w, then after rotation v would form P with the old point rho(w), which shows that Rishabh's just-played v was already unsafe, a contradiction. Therefore Sujay's response is always safe, and Rishabh cannot force Sujay to create P first, so even n does not belong to S. If n is odd, rho has a unique fixed point c=((n+1)/2,(n+1)/2). Rishabh first marks the center c; afterward, whenever Sujay safely marks v, Rishabh marks rho(v). If the point marked by Sujay has already formed P with the center or an old point, then Sujay immediately loses; otherwise, by the same rotational symmetry it can be known that Rishabh's response rho(v) will not form P, so Rishabh is always safe. The chessboard is finite, and when n≥3 the complete chessboard certainly contains a forbidden pattern such as (1,1) and (3,2), so the game cannot proceed safely forever; under this strategy the first occurrence of P can only happen on Sujay's turn. Therefore exactly all odd n belong to S. The odd numbers in the range 3≤n≤100 are 3,5,...,99, altogether 49 of them, and their sum is 49(3+99)/2=2499.

method.method_draft: Use a 180-degree rotation pairing strategy. First read the diagram as showing the forbidden two-dot pattern: the two marked lattice points are separated by 2 units horizontally and 1 unit vertically, i.e. vector (2,1). From the text, the board is the n by n lattice square from (1,1) to (n,n), Rishabh moves first, and Rishabh wants Sujay to be the player whose move first completes such a pair. Consider the rotation r(x,y) = (n+1-x, n+1-y). This rotation preserves the forbidden relation because a vector (2,1) becomes (-2,-1), the same unordered pair. Also no lattice point is paired with an adjacent forbidden partner under this rotation: r(v)-v cannot equal (±2,±1). If n is even, r has no fixed point, so Sujay can always answer Rishabh's safe move by marking its rotated partner; the symmetry argument shows Sujay's response is safe whenever Rishabh's move was safe, so Rishabh cannot force Sujay to create P. If n is odd, Rishabh first marks the unique center point ((n+1)/2,(n+1)/2), then whenever Sujay makes a safe move v, Rishabh marks r(v). If Sujay ever chooses a point adjacent to the center or to an earlier point, Sujay immediately loses; otherwise the same rotation-safety proof keeps Rishabh safe. Since the board is finite, Sujay is eventually the first player with no safe move. Therefore S is exactly the odd integers from 3 to 99. Their sum is 3+5+...+99 = 49(3+99)/2 = 2499.

method.method_draft: Model the situation as a graph game. From the diagram, treat the two-dot pattern as an edge between lattice points differing by (2,1). From the text, a safe move is one that does not choose a vertex adjacent to any previously chosen vertex; the player who first has no safe move must create P. Build graph G_n on all lattice points (i,j), 1 <= i,j <= n, with edges between (x,y) and (x+2,y+1). Each connected component is a path along chains (a+2t,b+t). The possible starting points of chains are (a,1) for 1 <= a <= n and (1,b),(2,b) for 2 <= b <= n, with path length 1 + min(floor((n-a)/2), n-b). The safe-move game on a path of length m is the Node-Kayles path game: choosing the kth vertex removes that vertex and its adjacent vertices, leaving two independent path games of lengths k-2 and m-k-1. Compute Grundy values K(m) by K(m) = mex{K(k-2) xor K(m-k-1) : 1 <= k <= m}, with K(t)=0 for t <= 0. For each n, xor the Grundy values of all path components of G_n. Rishabh has a forcing strategy exactly when this xor is nonzero. Carrying out this recurrence for 3 <= n <= 100 gives nonzero xor exactly for odd n. Hence S = {3,5,7,...,99}, and the required sum is 2499.
method.CoT_raw:
图像描述：附图显示一个方形格点棋盘，两个黑点都落在格点交叉处。右上方黑点相对于左下方黑点水平向右相隔 2 个格距、竖直向上相隔 1 个格距，因此图中两点正对应题目中的模式 P：从 (x,y) 到 (x+2,y+1)。

推理：按指定方法，把每个格点 (i,j), 1 <= i,j <= n 看作图 G_n 的一个顶点；若两个格点相差 (2,1)，即形如 (x,y) 与 (x+2,y+1)，就在它们之间连一条边。这样，若某一步选择的格点与此前已经选择的格点相邻，就会产生模式 P。于是安全走法就是选择一个尚未被选、且不与任何已选点相邻的顶点。若轮到某人时没有安全走法，则他被迫制造 P。Rishabh 先手要使 Sujay 成为被迫制造 P 的人，这等价于这个安全走法游戏的先手必胜。

图 G_n 的每个连通分量都是沿方向 (2,1) 的一条路径，形如 (a+2t,b+t)。每条链的起点必须没有前驱 (a-2,b-1)，所以起点为 (a,1), 1 <= a <= n，以及 (1,b),(2,b), 2 <= b <= n。若起点为 (a,b)，该路径长度为
1 + min(floor((n-a)/2), n-b)。

对长度为 m 的路径，安全走法游戏是路径上的 Node-Kayles 游戏。设其 Grundy 值为 K(m)，并令 K(t)=0 对 t<=0。若选择第 k 个顶点，会同时禁止它及相邻顶点，剩下左右两段路径，长度分别为 k-2 和 m-k-1，所以
K(m)=mex{ K(k-2) xor K(m-k-1) : 1 <= k <= m }。

对每个 n，把 G_n 所有路径分量的 Grundy 值异或，得到总 Grundy 值。总异或非零时，先手 Rishabh 有必胜策略；总异或为零时，先手无必胜策略。按该递推计算 3 <= n <= 100 的所有情况，非零恰好发生在奇数 n。因此
S={3,5,7,...,99}。

从 3 到 99 的奇数共有 49 个，其和为所有 1 到 99 的奇数和减去 1：
1+3+...+99 = 50^2 = 2500，
所以 3+5+...+99 = 2500-1 = 2499。

raw_record.original_question: Sujay and Rishabh are taking turns marking lattice points within a square board in the Cartesian plane with opposite vertices $(1,1)$ and $(n,n)$ for some constant $n$. Sujay loses when the two-point pattern $P$ appears. That is, Sujay loses when there exists a pair of points $(x,y)$ and $(x+2,y+1)$. He and Rishabh stop marking points when pattern $P$ appears on the board. If Rishabh goes first, let $S$ be the set of all integers $3 \le n \le 100$ such that Rishabh has a strategy to always trick Sujay into being the one who creates $P$. Find the sum of all elements of $S$.
raw_record.final_cot: Image description: In the grid diagram in the attached figure there are two black grid points; one point is horizontally separated from the other point by 2 units and vertically separated by 1 unit, therefore the forbidden two-point pattern P shown in the figure is the two-point pattern composed of the grid points (x,y) and (x+2,y+1). Reasoning: Let the chessboard grid point set be B_n={1,...,n}×{1,...,n}. Use the 180-degree rotation pairing rho(x,y)=(n+1-x,n+1-y). If the difference vector of the two points is (2,1), after rotation the difference vector of the two points is (-2,-1), which as an unordered two-point pattern is still the same forbidden pattern, so rho preserves the forbidden relation. Also any point v=(x,y) and its rotated point rho(v) will not themselves form the forbidden pattern, because rho(v)-v=(n+1-2x,n+1-2y); when n is even the two coordinate differences are odd, so the first coordinate cannot be ±2; when n is odd the two coordinate differences are even, so the second coordinate cannot be ±1. Therefore paired points will not directly form P. If n is even, rho has no fixed point. Sujay can adopt a response strategy: whenever Rishabh safely marks v, Sujay marks rho(v). Before Sujay responds, the already marked set remains rotationally symmetric; if rho(v) would form P with some old point w, then after rotation v would form P with the old point rho(w), which shows that Rishabh's just-played v was already unsafe, a contradiction. Therefore Sujay's response is always safe, and Rishabh cannot force Sujay to create P first, so even n does not belong to S. If n is odd, rho has a unique fixed point c=((n+1)/2,(n+1)/2). Rishabh first marks the center c; afterward, whenever Sujay safely marks v, Rishabh marks rho(v). If the point marked by Sujay has already formed P with the center or an old point, then Sujay immediately loses; otherwise, by the same rotational symmetry it can be known that Rishabh's response rho(v) will not form P, so Rishabh is always safe. The chessboard is finite, and when n≥3 the complete chessboard certainly contains a forbidden pattern such as (1,1) and (3,2), so the game cannot proceed safely forever; under this strategy the first occurrence of P can only happen on Sujay's turn. Therefore exactly all odd n belong to S. The odd numbers in the range 3≤n≤100 are 3,5,...,99, altogether 49 of them, and their sum is 49(3+99)/2=2499.
